processing: Sun-dried Yunnan leaf steamed and pressed into a mushroom or heart shape with a short stem. Traditional jincha hid the coarsest stems and broken leaf in the core with better leaf outside, while later recipes moved to finer material.
harvest_season: Not tied to one prized picking; it is a blended, pressed product with the production date on the pack.
appearance_dry: A small mushroom-shaped piece with a short stem, tightly pressed and wrapped in white cotton paper, with a rice-paper label pressed into the surface.
appearance_liquor: An orange-yellow, clear liquor after some years of dry storage, going by a comparable Baoyan jincha.
appearance_wet: Fairly broken, uneven leaf that stays lively and supple.
taste_profile: Going by a comparable decade-old Baoyan jincha: bitter on entry with lasting astringency, then a quick returning sweetness and a thick feel. Young pieces can carry smoke, which fades with storage.

brewing.notes: Break the piece up, rinse twice and keep steeps short, since the broken leaf extracts quickly. It can also be boiled, as it was traditionally for butter tea.

vintage_note: Sold by production year, both new and with some age, and a raw version is the classic with ripe ones also made under the Baoyan label. Around ten years of good dry storage is a sensible target. Check wrapper details and dates, since Xiaguan's output has been imitated.
description:
This is a mushroom-shaped pressed sheng from the Xiaguan factory in Dali, one of the Baoyan-brand jincha. Jincha means tight tea, and its heart-like shape earned it nicknames such as mushroom head and ox-heart tea.

It was made for Tibetan areas, where it was boiled into butter tea. So the old recipe was practical and rough, with low-grade stems and broken leaf packed in the middle. Modern jincha has moved towards finer leaf that suits steeping. The short stem is said to be held between the fingers during offerings and when presenting a hada.

Expect a strong tea. A comparable piece stored for nine years opens bitter and grippy, then turns sweet fast, with an orange-yellow liquor and a thick feel. Keep the steeps short and do not be alarmed by broken leaf.

It is sold by year, so buy with the date in mind. Fresh pieces can be sharp and smoky, and a decade in dry storage does them good.

To understand it, try a plain Xiaguan tuocha next to it: same factory, quite a different idea.
history:
Jincha appeared in Yunnan after tuocha. The Yunnan Provincial Tea Company unified it under the Baoyan brand in 1949, and pieces from the Menghai, Xiaguan, Jinggu and Yanjin factories carried a Baoyan label. In 1986 production passed entirely to Xiaguan, according to trade writing.

The Banchan name points to the Panchen Lama, but little reliable detail is documented about how and when this particular name was attached. The Baoyan Banchan jincha is praised for careful making and an old-fashioned form, and is known mainly through trade writing.
